title: API Inspector Training in the Midwest: Online Exam Prep
description: Where API 510, 570, 580 and 653 inspectors work across Illinois, Indiana, Ohio, Michigan and Minnesota, and how to prepare online around winter and turnarounds.
h1: API inspector training for the Midwest: refineries, pipeline terminals and cold-climate inspection
html:
The Midwest runs some of the largest refineries in the country, a dense web of crude and products pipelines and the tank terminals that sit between them. Every one of those sites needs people who can read a thickness survey, set an inspection interval and defend it to a regulator, which is the work API 510, API 570, API 580 and API 653 certification is built around. This page is for technicians, operators, engineers and inspection supervisors in Illinois, Indiana, Ohio, Michigan, Minnesota, Wisconsin and the St. Louis and Kansas City areas who want to sit an API examination. It sets out where the work is, what a Midwest winter adds to it, which state and city rules sit beside an API certificate, and how to prepare with a self-paced online course while holding down a plant job.

Where API inspectors work in the Midwest

Refining in the region clusters in four places: the southern tip of Lake Michigan, the Mississippi River above St. Louis, north-west Ohio and south-east Michigan, and the Twin Cities. Around each cluster sit pipeline tank farms, products terminals, chemical plants and the contractors and inspection companies that serve them. The table names sites that operators publish themselves; capacities are the figures those operators state.

Ownership in the region keeps moving. Phillips 66 has operated Wood River since the WRB joint venture began in 2007 and agreed in September 2025 to buy Cenovus's half of it; Cenovus took full control of the Toledo refinery it once shared with bp. A change of owner rarely changes the equipment, but it often changes the inspection procedures, the damage mechanism reviews and the record system the inspector works in, so candidates who can learn a new programme quickly are the ones contractors keep calling back.

Matching the certification to the Midwest job

Most Midwest candidates are choosing between API 510 and API 570, because the refineries above carry thousands of vessels and many miles of unit piping. Pipeline terminals such as the Hartford farm, and the tank fields inside the refineries, are API 653 territory. API 580 is the credential for people who build or audit risk-based inspection programmes, and holders of a current 510, 570 or 653 certificate qualify for it automatically.

  • API 510 suits inspectors who look after columns, drums, exchangers, reactors and the relief devices on them. The eligibility rules and exam outline are on the API 510 certification page.
  • API 570 suits inspectors who own circuits of process piping, injection points, dead legs and insulated lines. See the API 570 certification page.
  • API 653 suits terminal and tank-field inspectors: shell, bottom, roof and foundation, plus the repair and alteration rules. See the API 653 certification page.
  • API 580 suits integrity engineers and inspection leads who maintain an RBI programme. Atlantis also runs remote RBI studies, described on its Chicago-area RBI page.

If you cannot decide, the comparison of which API certification to take first walks through the choice by job.

Winter, turnarounds and the Midwest inspection calendar

A Gulf Coast inspector can plan outdoor work almost any month. A Midwest inspector cannot. Owners tend to push tank out-of-service work, large insulation-removal scopes and hydrotests away from the deep-winter months, and the planned maintenance season leans heavily on spring: the U.S. Energy Information Administration notes that planned refinery maintenance generally peaks during late February and March. For an API candidate that calendar matters twice. It sets when you are busiest, and it sets which code questions you will meet first once you start work.

Cold weather brings its own damage. Water trapped in dead legs, low points and idle bypasses can freeze and split a line. Leaking steam tracing soaks insulation, and carbon steel kept between roughly 10°F and 350°F under wet insulation is in the band where corrosion under insulation develops, which in a Midwest plant includes lines that cycle through freezing and thawing several times a winter. Frost heave and poor drainage under tank pads show up later as settlement and bottom corrosion. None of this is unusual to an experienced Midwest inspector, but the exam expects you to know where each code tells you to look harder.

Cold-climate code points worth practising

The API exam is national, so it does not test Midwest weather. It does test the clauses that cold service brings into play, and Midwest candidates who have lived those clauses tend to find them easier to answer.

Brittle fracture in API 653

API 653 asks the inspector to assess older tanks for brittle fracture risk. The decision points are the nominal thickness of the thickest shell plate, with half an inch as a key threshold; a shell metal temperature of 60°F, at or above which API reports no known brittle fracture failures; whether the tank has been hydrotested or has already run at its maximum fill height at the lowest expected one-day mean temperature; and the exemption curve for plates of unknown toughness. A change of service to a lower temperature or a heavier product reopens the assessment. Take a Minnesota crude tank whose bottom course is three-quarters of an inch thick, built from steel with no toughness records, holding cold product through January. Neither the thickness rule nor the 60°F rule clears it, so the answer turns on its test and operating history and on where it falls on the exemption curve.

Hydrotest temperature for a vessel

ASME Section VIII recommends that the metal temperature during a hydrostatic test be kept at least 30°F above the vessel's minimum design metal temperature. A drum stamped with an MDMT of minus 20°F should therefore be tested with the metal at 10°F or warmer, and one stamped at plus 10°F needs 40°F or warmer. In a Midwest February, that can decide whether the test water must be heated, which is exactly the kind of practical consequence an API 510 question likes to hide inside a scenario.

Dead legs and insulated piping in API 570

API 570 treats dead legs, injection points and insulated systems as places that need targeted inspection rather than the circuit's average treatment. Practise reading those clauses and the related recommended practice, API RP 574, until you can say which locations get extra readings and why. A wider walk-through of CUI inspection methods is in the CUI detection guide.

State and city rules beside an API certificate

An API certificate shows that you know the inspection codes. It does not license you to sign off a pressure vessel under a state law, and Midwest jurisdictions differ from one state line to the next.

  • Illinois: the Office of the State Fire Marshal's Division of Boiler and Pressure Vessel Safety registers and inspects boilers and pressure vessels that are not exempt, using state inspectors and commissioned insurance-company inspectors, and the state act provides for owner-user inspection programmes. The act does not apply in cities of more than 500,000 inhabitants, which takes Chicago out of it; the city's Boiler Inspection Bureau inspects boilers and unfired pressure vessels under the Municipal Code.
  • Indiana: the Boilers and Pressure Vessels Section of the Department of Homeland Security issues operating permits based on inspections by Indiana-licensed boiler and pressure vessel inspectors, under the rules at 675 IAC 30.
  • Ohio: boilers may not run until the state superintendent issues a certificate of operation, and inspections are made by commissioned inspectors.
  • Michigan: the boiler division of the Department of Licensing and Regulatory Affairs certifies boilers.

The practical lesson for a candidate is that the API credential and the state commission are separate things, and many Midwest owner-user inspectors need both. The course prepares you for the API examination; it does not cover the commission examinations.

Preparing for an API exam on a Midwest shift pattern

Most people preparing in this region are working rotating shifts, travelling between turnarounds or covering for colleagues who are. The course is self-paced for that reason, and an instructor answers your questions as you work through the material. Several patterns work well here:

  1. Pick an exam window that falls after your busiest season, not during it. If your site's spring turnaround runs through March, aim at a later window and use the winter for the bulk of the reading.
  2. Use the quiet weeks of winter for the heaviest code reading: Section VIII for API 510, B31.3 for API 570, API 650 for API 653.
  3. During a turnaround, keep a short list of questions from the job itself, such as a reading you did not understand or a repair rule you had to look up, and send them to the instructor when you are back.
  4. Sit at least one full timed practice paper in the final weeks, closed-book and open-book halves together, to find out how a long examination day feels.

API 510, API 570 and API 653 are taken in person at Prometric test centres, and Prometric lists centres in and around the region's cities. Seats are first-come, first-served, so book early in the window. API's exam page lists API 580 among the examinations that can be taken by remote proctoring. API reports scores on a scale from 200 to 500 with 400 as the passing score.

Eligibility routes for Midwest candidates

API administers the examinations, sets the eligibility rules and issues the certification. For API 510, API 570 and API 653, it combines education with inspection-related experience gained in the last ten years while employed by or under contract to an authorized inspection agency. Engineering graduates need the least experience and candidates without formal education the most, with two-year and high-school routes between them. In the Midwest that tends to mean:

  • NDT technicians at contract inspection companies, whose thickness surveys and examinations count when they are part of inspection activities as the code describes them;
  • refinery operators and maintenance technicians who move into an owner-user inspection department and start accumulating qualifying time there;
  • welders and fabricators, whose fabrication and repair experience with the equipment can count towards the two-year, high-school and no-formal-education routes, provided at least a year of it is supervision or performance of inspection;
  • process and mechanical engineers, who can qualify after a year of supervising or performing inspection work.

Experience is documented on the application and verified by API, so check the detail on the certification page for your code before you count your years.

Employers sponsoring Midwest candidates

Refineries, terminal operators and inspection contractors often sponsor several candidates in the same year, sometimes for different codes. Fees are quoted on request and the enquiry can cover the whole group. Each candidate still applies to API individually and sits the examination individually. Atlantis's other training for the region includes ASNT SNT-TC-1A NDT courses, with local detail on the pages for Chicago, Toledo, Detroit, St. Louis and Minneapolis, and the AWS CWI exam-prep course, with city pages for Chicago and Detroit. In the US, Atlantis performs UT, MT, PT and VT inspection and does not perform radiography.

faq.q: Is there an Atlantis classroom in Chicago, Detroit or Minneapolis?
faq.a: No. There is no Atlantis classroom in Chicago, Detroit, Minneapolis or anywhere else in the Midwest; Atlantis's offices are in Houston and Hyderabad. The API exam-prep course is studied online at your own pace, with an instructor answering your questions. The examination itself is sat at a Prometric test centre for API 510, API 570 and API 653.

faq.q: Can I keep studying through a winter turnaround?
faq.a: Yes. Because the course is self-paced, you can stop during a turnaround and pick up where you left off, and the questions you collect on the job make good material for the instructor. What you cannot move is the exam window: API schedules each examination within a set window with its own application deadline, so choose a window that leaves you a clear run after your busiest weeks.

faq.q: Does an API 510 certificate let me inspect pressure vessels in Illinois or Indiana?
faq.a: Not by itself. API certification shows you know the inspection code, but state law decides who may inspect for registration and permits. Illinois uses state and commissioned insurance-company inspectors and provides for owner-user programmes, Indiana requires Indiana-licensed inspectors for operating permits, and Chicago runs its own Boiler Inspection Bureau. Many owner-user inspectors hold an API certificate and a state commission.

faq.q: I inspect tanks at a pipeline terminal near St. Louis. Which API certification should I take?
faq.a: API 653 is written for aboveground storage tanks built to API 650 and its predecessor, so it fits terminal work on shells, bottoms, roofs and foundations. If you also look after the terminal's transfer piping and manifolds, API 570 is the natural second step. The API 653 certification page sets out the eligibility and exam format.

faq.q: Are cold-climate topics such as brittle fracture on the API exams?
faq.a: The exams draw on the codes listed in the Body of Knowledge and Publications Effectivity Sheet for your window, not on regional weather. Those codes include clauses that cold service brings into play, such as the brittle fracture assessment in API 653 and the hydrotest temperature recommendation in ASME Section VIII. Check the effectivity sheet for your window to see which editions are examined.

faq.q: I am a refinery operator. Does my plant experience count towards eligibility?
faq.a: It can help. For the two-year, high-school and no-formal-education routes, API counts experience in the design, fabrication, repair, operation or inspection of the equipment, but every route also needs at least one year spent supervising or performing inspection, and the experience must be gained while employed by or under contract to an authorized inspection agency. Operators who move into an owner-user inspection department usually build that inspection year there. Keep records of the work as you do it.

faq.q: Can I take the API 580 exam from home?
faq.a: API's exam scheduling page lists API 580 among the examinations available through remote proctoring on Prometric's ProProctor platform, while API 510, API 570 and API 653 must be taken at a test centre. Confirm the delivery options for your window when you apply, because API sets them.

faq.q: Can our refinery sponsor a group of inspectors for different API codes?
faq.a: Yes. Send one enquiry listing how many candidates you have for each code and the exam windows they are aiming at, and the quote covers the group. Each person studies at their own pace with access to the instructor, applies to API individually and sits the examination individually.
